title: Po: one device is a sense amp — tunnel-diode Goto latch
idea: Po: a sense amplifier made of one device. Replace the ~10-transistor cross-coupled latch with a series Goto pair of resonant/Esaki tunnel diodes per bitline, biased by a clocked supply so the midpoint snaps to one of its two NDR-stable states as set by the few-mV charge-sharing signal; a single pass transistor writes the snapped state back for restore.
why: Periphery (#7): SA strip area shrinks ~50-60%, which buys shorter bitlines (more SA strips per mm) for ~1.5x signal; ps-class NDR switching also trims tRCD.

title: Po: sense amps take turns — 1:8 charge-parked sensing
idea: Po: a bank with one-eighth of its sense amps. After activation, isolation gates park each bitline's charge-shared signal on the bitline itself; one SA serves 8 bitlines through a mux, sensing and writing back group by group in ~2 ns slots, with the requested column group always sensed first.
why: Periphery (#7): SA+equalizer strips (~15-20% of die) shrink ~7/8, ~10% better cost per bit; first-access tRCD unchanged, only tRAS grows. Parked charge decays over microseconds, so the 16 ns window is safe.

title: Po: biased sense amps that favor the decaying state
idea: Po: a sense amp that is deliberately unfair. Because only the charged state leaks (true cells toward '0', anti cells toward '1'), give every SA a designed offset (asymmetric device sizing or a shifted bitline precharge) toward the leaky state, with the skew direction flipped per mat to match true/anti-cell layout in open-bitline arrays.
why: Refresh (#3): the full-swing non-leaking state has margin to spare, so lending it to the decaying state extends the retention tail ~1.5-2x, cutting refresh energy (46 fJ/bit) and bandwidth loss proportionally.

title: Po: let the sense amp guess — early fire plus ECC
idea: Po: a sense amp allowed to be wrong. Fire the latch at ~40% of the normal signal-development time and accept raw bit errors ~1e-5, then correct with a strong on-die BCH code over 512-bit words computed in the periphery during the column access.
why: Capacitor wall (#1): either tRCD falls ~30% or Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~3 fF at today's timing, avoiding AR-115 pillars; the ECC logic costs ~3% die, far less than a capacitor-etch generation.

title: Po: bitlines live on the wafer's backside
idea: Po: a bitline on the other side of the wafer. After front-side capacitor and buried-wordline formation, bond to a carrier, thin to ~500 nm, and pattern bitlines and the SA strip on the backside, contacting access-transistor drains through nano-vias, so bitlines never run between capacitor pillars or beside wordlines.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and periphery (#7): bitline capacitance drops ~40% (no BL-to-storage-node or BL-to-WL coupling), giving ~1.6x signal per fF of Cs, and SAs get a whole wafer face of area.

title: Po: memory trims its own readers via dummy cells
idea: Po: memory that calibrates the circuits that read it. At power-up each SA's offset is measured by repeatedly sensing balanced bitlines, and a correction charge is written into a dedicated dummy cell on that bitline pair; before every sense the dummy wordline fires and pre-biases the bitline by exactly that offset, refreshed alongside normal refresh.
why: Periphery (#7) and capacitor wall (#1): cancels ~80% of SA Vt mismatch, so SA devices can be ~3x smaller or Cs ~30% lower; trim storage costs one row per subarray instead of fuses or analog trim DACs.

title: Po: wordlines count themselves — analog hammer integrator cell
idea: Po: a wordline that keeps its own tally. Each sub-wordline driver gets one extra DRAM-style cell coupled to its wordline through a tiny capacitor so every activation deposits a fixed charge quantum; when that integrator crosses a threshold during the row group's refresh, its neighbors are flagged for targeted refresh and the integrator is reset.
why: Row hammer (#9) at ~1k activations: exact per-row counting at roughly one cell per row instead of SRAM counter tables or controller tracking, and it keeps working as thresholds fall further.

title: Po: wordlines on springs — stepwise adiabatic charge-recycling drivers
idea: Po: a wordline that bounces back for free. Drive each global/main wordline through a stepwise adiabatic charger, 4-6 on-die tank capacitors switched in sequence, so the ~3 V wordline rises and falls in small steps and returns most of its charge to the tanks instead of dumping it to ground.
why: Voltage floor (#10): wordline CV^2 energy falls ~60-75%, which also unloads the VPP charge pump and shrinks it (periphery #7).

title: Po: weakest cousins schedule refresh — canary-cell mats
idea: Po: memory that is told when to refresh by its weakest relatives. Each mat holds one row of canary cells with deliberately shrunk capacitors (~60% Cs), sensed by the normal SAs at each refresh; the mat's refresh interval doubles while all canaries hold and halves on the first canary failure, tracking process and temperature automatically.
why: Refresh (#3): most mats can run 2-4x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy and the 10-20% bandwidth loss at <0.2% area, with per-mat rather than per-die worst-case margins.

title: Po: no reference — read, write midlevel, read again
idea: Po: a sense amp with no reference. Charge-share the cell onto the bitline and hold the result on sample cap A, write VDD/2 into the cell, re-open the wordline and hold the second result on cap B, then compare A vs B; both samples traverse the identical path, so wordline kickback, bitline-pair imbalance and open-bitline layout mismatch cancel.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and periphery (#7): removes ~10-20 mV of systematic offset, allowing ~30% lower Cs or 2x longer bitlines (half the SA strips); the extra latency suits a density-optimized capacity tier.

title: Po: bitlines never precharge — rail-held transition sensing
idea: Po: bitlines that never return to VDD/2. Each bitline stays at the full rail left by the last restore; on the next activation an AC-coupled detector sees either no step (new bit equals held rail) or a full charge-sharing step, and the latch, knowing the held rail, decodes 'same/different' into the new bit.
why: Destructive read (#8) energy: removes equalization and tRP (~14 ns), and bitlines only swing when consecutive rows differ, ~50% bitline energy saving on random data and more on correlated data.

title: Po: read cells like a camera — single-slope ternary ADC
idea: Po: memory read like an image sensor. Store three charge levels per cell; a bank-wide voltage ramp and a counter are broadcast to all columns, and each column comparator latches the count when its bitline crosses the ramp, exactly as CMOS image-sensor column ADCs do, then a 2-bit column DAC restores the level.
why: Density and capacitor wall (#1): 1.58 bits per capacitor pillar (~50% more bits per array area); the shared ramp/counter keeps per-column overhead to one comparator and a small latch.

title: Po: bitlines amplify themselves — oxide TFT segment preamps
idea: Po: a bitline with gain built into it. Cut each bitline into 32-cell local segments, each sensed by a BEOL IGZO thin-film gain transistor stacked above the capacitor array whose gate is the segment node; the tiny segment capacitance (~1/8 of a full bitline) gives ~6x larger swing that the TFT converts into current on a global bitline.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and 3D (#2): Cs can drop from ~5 fF to ~1 fF at equal signal, enabling shallow capacitors that suit stacked tiers.

title: Po: the charge pump lives in the package
idea: Po: a DRAM die with no charge pumps. Generate VPP (~3 V) and the negative wordline bias in a package-level GaN or deep-trench-capacitor integrated-passive converter at ~85% efficiency and deliver them through dedicated bumps or hybrid-bond pads, deleting on-die pumps and their decoupling capacitors.
why: Periphery (#7) and voltage floor (#10): on-die pumps and decaps take ~5-8% of die and run ~30-40% efficient; moving them out frees area and roughly halves VPP energy.

title: Po: an array die that cannot decode
idea: Po: an array die that knows no addresses. Row/column predecoding, redundancy CAMs, refresh counters and command logic move to a hybrid-bonded logic-node base die, which drives pre-decoded one-hot group selects through ~1 um-pitch bonds; the array die keeps only sub-wordline drivers, SAs and final pass gates.
why: Periphery (#7): array-die periphery drops from ~49% to ~25-30%, ~35% more bits per array wafer, while the moved logic is ~5x denser on a logic node.

title: Po: one amplifier hears sixteen bitlines via CCD transfer
idea: Po: bitlines without sense amps. Borrow CCD readout: short bitlines end in a buried-channel charge-transfer register that clocks each cell's charge packet losslessly to a floating-diffusion amplifier shared by 16 bitlines, which senses it non-destructively and writes it back through the reverse transfer.
why: Periphery (#7) and capacitor wall (#1): 16:1 fewer sense circuits, and charge-domain readout is not divided by bitline capacitance, so the full Cs charge is sensed; transfer time (~0.5 ns/stage) is the price.

title: Po: array runs on 0.4 V — Marx-stacked bitline sampling
idea: Po: an array that runs on 0.4 V. Drop VARY to ~0.4 V; after charge sharing, the bitline differential is sampled onto four small capacitors in parallel, which are then switched into series like a Marx generator, presenting ~4x the voltage to a latch that restores to 0.4 V.
why: Voltage floor (#10): array CV^2 energy falls ~6x vs 1 V while the Marx stack recovers the voltage margin lost to the low swing.

title: Po: the periphery is the product — open bonded interface
idea: Po: a DRAM company that makes no memory cells. Define an open JEDEC-style hybrid-bonding contract between array wafers and periphery wafers (pad map, analog bitline/wordline electrical specs, timing), so any foundry or new U.S. entrant can build periphery dies that pair with any vendor's array wafers.
why: Capital (#4) and U.S. manufacturability: periphery needs mature logic fabs, not $15B DRAM fabs; opens the ~49% periphery share of the die to competition and second sourcing.

title: Po: never open a full row — column-gated sub-wordlines
idea: Po: a row that is never fully opened. Merge ACT and RD into one command carrying row and column address, and AND the column-group select into each sub-wordline driver so only the ~1 kb segment containing the requested line is activated and sensed.
why: Overfetch (#8): 128x overfetch falls to ~16x for random access, ~5x lower activate energy per useful bit; fewer opened cells also cut aggressor activity (row hammer #9).

title: Po: grade chips like diamonds — per-bank sense-margin timing
idea: Po: memory graded stone by stone. At test, measure sense margin and retention per bank and write per-bank tRCD/tRAS/tREFI tables into SPD; controllers run each bank at its own timing, so dies that miss a single global spec on a few banks are sold instead of scrapped.
why: Usable supply: recovers ~5-10% of dies that fail global bins and gives ~15% average latency gain on strong banks with no fab change.

title: Po: rows only know 'next' — token-ring subarray refresh
idea: Po: a decoder that only knows 'next'. Add a display-style shift-register gate-driver chain (2-3 transistors per row, like gate-on-array in LCD panels) beside each subarray that passes a refresh token row to row, so idle subarrays refresh independently of the address decoder while others serve accesses.
why: Refresh (#3): hides the 10-20% bandwidth loss at 32-64 Gb through subarray-parallel refresh with ~1-2% area and no decoder contention.

title: Po: the bit is when, not how much — wordline ramp
idea: Po: memory read by timing. Ramp the wordline slowly: an access transistor holding '0' turns on near Vwl=Vt while one holding '1' turns on only near Vt+VDD/2, so a per-bitline edge detector timestamps the first bitline movement against the ramp and decodes data from turn-on time and direction, largely independent of Cs.
why: Capacitor wall (#1): sensing becomes tolerant of small and variable Cs (~2 fF cells), and slow wordline edges reduce coupling disturbance (row hammer #9).

title: Po: only one transistor species — array-device periphery
idea: Po: a DRAM with only one kind of transistor. Build sense amps, sub-wordline drivers and local logic from the same buried-channel/vertical access transistor used in the array (plus a wider-footprint variant), deleting the separate HKMG periphery module.
why: Capital (#4): removes ~10-15 masks and the high-k/metal-gate module, ~8-12% wafer cost and less hafnium; slower periphery is offset with more parallel banks.

title: Po: sense with the transistor DRAM abandoned — lateral Si BJT
idea: Po: a bipolar memory reader. Place a lateral npn preamp pair (boron/phosphorus-doped silicon only, no high-k, no metal gate) at each SA input; BJT Vbe matching (~0.3 mV sigma vs ~5 mV for small MOSFETs) and higher gm resolve millivolt signals before a cheap MOS latch.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and periphery (#7): ~10x lower offset lets Cs drop ~40% or bitlines double in length (half the SA strips), using only Si, B, P.

title: Po: a sense amp with moving parts — bistable Si nanobeam
idea: Po: a sense amplifier with moving parts. A buckled, bistable single-crystal Si nanobeam (~200 nm long) sits between electrodes tied to the bitline pair; the differential tips it into one well, where it mechanically latches and touches a restore electrode, giving zero leakage and zero standby power.
why: Periphery (#7) and idle power: zero SA leakage in a ~0.05 um^2 footprint from silicon alone; 10-50 ns switching restricts it to capacity tiers.

title: Po: the sense amp remembers its offset — AlBN ferroelectric trim
idea: Po: a sense amplifier with memory. One input transistor of each SA gets a thin ferroelectric aluminum boron nitride gate layer; at test the measured offset is cancelled by one program pulse that permanently shifts that transistor's Vt, with no fuses or trim DACs.
why: Periphery (#7) and capacitor wall (#1): non-volatile per-SA offset cancellation lets SA devices shrink ~3x or cuts required signal ~40%, using Al, B, N instead of Hf-based HZO.

title: Po: gain from a negative capacitor — ZrO2 NC input pair
idea: Po: a transistor whose gate amplifies before its channel does. Insert a stabilized ferroelectric ZrO2 layer (Zr is abundant; no Hf) in series with the SA input-pair gate oxide, capacitance-matched so negative capacitance gives ~2x internal voltage gain and sub-60 mV/decade turn-on.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and voltage floor (#10): ~2x SA input gm per area, so ~30% less signal or a lower SA supply, without hafnium.

title: Po: shrink the capacitor to amplify — MOS varactor parametric gain
idea: Po: an amplifier with no gain transistor. Sample the bitline differential onto a pair of silicon MOS varactors held in accumulation, then pulse them into depletion so their capacitance falls ~5x while charge is conserved, raising the differential voltage ~5x before the latch.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and periphery (#7): ~5x voltage gain before any matched transistor, so SA offset matters ~5x less; silicon and oxide only.

title: Po: wordlines latch themselves — vertical Si thyristor drivers
idea: Po: a wordline driver that needs only a nudge. Replace each sub-wordline driver's high-voltage CMOS pair with a vertical p-n-p-n silicon thyristor at wordline pitch: a small decoder pulse triggers it, it regenerates and holds the wordline high through a shared weak bleed, and a common reset pulse turns all off.
why: Periphery (#7): sub-wordline driver strips (~10% of die) shrink ~3x because vertical thyristors need no thick-oxide PMOS or well spacing; Si, B, P only.

title: Po: banks chosen by pitch — AlN resonator select tones
idea: Po: a decoder that listens for its note. Each bank or subarray group enable is gated by an AlN thin-film acoustic resonator with a unique frequency on one shared RF select line; a single-tone burst wakes only the matching group through a rectifier, replacing trees of global decode wires and repeaters.
why: Periphery (#7): fewer global decode wires and repeaters and less routing congestion, using CMOS-compatible Al and N only.

title: Po: decoders woven into wiring — a-Si diode matrix
idea: Po: a decoder made of wire crossings. Build the row predecoder as a 1960s-style diode matrix, with hydrogenated amorphous-silicon p-i-n diodes deposited at the crossings of two BEOL aluminum levels above the array, so decoding uses metal-layer space instead of silicon area.
why: Periphery (#7) and capital (#4): moves ~3-5% of die (predecode) off silicon using Si and H deposited below 350 C on cheap tools.

title: Po: rust-and-zinc logic above the array — Cu2O/ZnO CMOS
idea: Po: periphery made of rust and zinc. Build complementary BEOL thin-film logic from p-type Cu2O and n-type Al-doped ZnO (no In or Ga) to host refresh counters, mode registers, test and redundancy logic stacked above the cell array.
why: Periphery (#7) and scarce resources: shifts ~5-8% of slow control logic into vertical space using only Cu, Zn, Al, O, avoiding IGZO's indium and gallium.

title: Po: the barrier grows itself — CuMn wiring, no Ta/Co/Ru
idea: Po: copper wiring that makes its own diffusion barrier. Use a Cu-0.5%Mn seed; on anneal Mn migrates to the dielectric interface and forms a ~2 nm MnSiOx barrier, replacing PVD Ta/TaN and Co/Ru liners in all periphery metal levels, with plain Al for top global levels.
why: Scarce resources: removes Ta, Co and Ru from periphery BEOL; the thinner barrier also adds ~15-20% copper cross-section in narrow lines, cutting RC.

title: Po: contacts made of silicon itself — silicide-capped epi plugs
idea: Po: a contact with no tungsten. Fill periphery contacts with in-situ-doped selective epitaxial silicon capped by self-aligned TiSi2/NiSi, topped by a TiN/Al local layer, eliminating WF6 CVD tungsten plugs throughout the periphery.
why: Scarce resources: removes tungsten (China ~80%) from contacts using Si, Ti, Ni, N, Al; epi plugs also tighten contact-resistance spread.

title: Po: the charge pump is a magnet — NiFe inductor boost
idea: Po: a charge pump replaced by a magnet. Generate VPP with an on-die inductive boost converter using thin-film permalloy (NiFe)-cored spiral inductors in the top Al/Cu level, switched at ~100 MHz by thick-oxide silicon devices.
why: Voltage floor (#10) and periphery (#7): ~75-85% efficient vs ~30-40% for charge pumps, halving VPP energy and freeing pump capacitor area; Ni and Fe are abundant.

title: Po: bitlines are the pump — idle-bank flying capacitors
idea: Po: a charge pump built from the memory's own wires. In idle banks, groups of bitlines (~100 fF each, millions available) are reconfigured through the equalizer switches plus a few added series switches into a switched-capacitor ladder that stacks charge up to VPP for the active banks' wordlines.
why: Periphery (#7): deletes most dedicated pump capacitor area by reusing capacitance already paid for; silicon only.

title: Po: gate from underneath — Hf-free back-gated FD-SOI periphery
idea: Po: transistors controlled from underneath. Build the periphery on thin-BOX FD-SOI with SiON front gates and TiN or doped-poly electrodes (no HfO2), using the back gate through the buried oxide for Vt control, and give each SA pair its own back-gate island biased to null its offset.
why: Scarce resources and capacitor wall (#1): avoids hafnium while recovering Vt tuning via body bias; per-SA back-bias trim cuts required signal; Si, O, N, Ti only.

title: Po: periphery made in a TV factory — LTPS glass chiplets
idea: Po: memory periphery from a display fab. Fabricate slow periphery (pumps, test, fuse/repair, ESD, power gating) as laser-crystallized poly-Si TFT circuits on Gen-6 glass panels, dice them into chiplets and bond them beside or under array dies.
why: Capital (#4) and U.S. manufacturability: panel lines process ~50x the area per tool-hour at a fraction of the cost per cm^2, and LTPS uses silicon only.

title: Po: a chip sold on its periodic table — abundance preference
idea: Po: a memory chip graded by its periodic table. Federal procurement and CHIPS rules give DRAM whose periphery and interconnect use only Earth-abundant elements (certified BOM: no W, Co, Ru, Ta, Hf, In, Ga) a 10% purchase preference and accelerated depreciation on the tooling.
why: Scarce resources and U.S. manufacturability: a demand signal that pays for the periphery material changes and insulates supply from tungsten and gallium export controls.

title: Po: the row buffer survives power-off — FeB/MgO shadow latches
idea: Po: open rows that survive power-off. Pair each SA with a Co-free FeB/MgO/FeB magnetic tunnel junction shadow latch on Ti/TiN seeds, written as a row closes, so SA and decoder strips can be fully power-gated between bursts and the row buffer restored in nanoseconds on wake.
why: Idle power (#3 share): periphery leakage drops close to zero during idle while open-row hits are kept; Fe, B, Mg, O, Ti only.

title: Po: a photon-counter sense amp — Geiger-mode silicon junction
idea: Po: a sense amp as sensitive as a photon counter. Gate a pair of small Si p+/n junctions just above breakdown (Geiger mode, as in a SPAD) during sensing; the bitline differential biases which side avalanches first, the avalanche current latches that side, and a doped-poly quench resistor resets it.
why: Periphery (#7) and capacitor wall (#1): ~1e5 intrinsic junction gain from two devices, so tiny signals suffice; Si, B, P only. Dark counts and afterpulsing are the risk.

title: Po: the chip forgets its repairs — off-die repair maps
idea: Po: a chip that does not remember where it is broken. Delete on-die e-fuse/antifuse banks and their HV programming; store row/column repair maps in module SPD flash or the controller, upload them at boot over a sideband into a small CAM per bank, and update them in the field as weak rows appear.
why: Periphery (#7) and usable supply: frees ~2-4% of die, removes silicide fuse links, and field-updatable repair raises effective yield and lifetime.

title: Po: dies talk without touching — inductive-coupled stack I/O
idea: Po: a memory stack with no data TSVs. Replace HBM data TSVs with vertically aligned on-die Cu/Al spiral coil pairs (inductive coupling through thinned dies), keeping only a few large power TSVs for supply.
why: HBM TSV tax (#6): removes most TSV keep-out area and the 20-30% TSV yield loss; coils use standard metal, no W fill or Ta liners.

title: Po: bitline capacitance is negative — active NIC cancellation
idea: Po: a bitline that pretends to be shorter. A small positive-feedback negative-impedance converter (cross-coupled Si MOS pair driving a coupling capacitor) at the bitline end synthesizes about -0.5 Cb during charge sharing, so the cell sees half the load and develops ~2x the voltage signal.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and periphery (#7): ~2x signal, or Cs ~50% lower, or twice the cells per bitline (half the SA strips), with plain Si CMOS and no exotic dielectric.

title: Po: every bitline wears a shield — coaxial poly-Si bitlines
idea: Po: a bitline wrapped like a TV cable. Form bitlines inside a grounded conformal doped poly-Si sleeve separated by an SiO2/air liner, so neighbor-bitline coupling and wordline kickback terminate on the shield; Cb rises ~15% but pattern-dependent noise (up to ~30% of sense margin) disappears.
why: Capacitor wall (#1) and density: ~15% net margin gain and tighter bitline pitch, using Si, O, N only.

title: Po: half the transistors missing — NMOS-only bootstrapped sense amp
idea: Po: a sense amp without PMOS. Use an NMOS cross-coupled latch for sensing and restore the high side through a capacitive bootstrap that lifts an NMOS pull-up gate above VDD for a few ns, eliminating the n-well, PMOS implants and well-to-well spacing in the SA strip.
why: Periphery (#7) and capital (#4): SA strips lose ~30% width from well spacing and drop a couple of implant masks; Si, B, P, SiO2 only.
